title: The Jumpy Goalkeeper
briefing: Sam, 13, is the goalkeeper. A shot comes straight at her face from close range; she blinks and her hands fly up and block it before she even knows what happened. Yet a slow, curling shot from far away went in last week while she “just watched it.”
question: Why did her body move faster than her thinking the first time — and not the second?

clues.title: The blink came first
clues.text: Her eyes shut before she saw the ball clearly. She did not choose to blink — it just happened.
clues.shows: a reaction that happened without any decision

clues.title: Hands up, no plan
clues.text: Her hands were already in front of her face by the time her mind “caught up” with what was happening.
clues.shows: the body acting before the thinking part knew

clues.title: Practice makes faster
clues.text: After two weeks of drills, her dive starts about a tenth of a second sooner than before.
clues.shows: that the deciding kind of reaction can be trained

visual.unit: s to start the dive, before → after drills

clues.title: Tired = slower
clues.text: At the end of a double practice she reacts noticeably later to the same drill — but she still blinks just as fast.
clues.shows: tiredness slowing decisions but not the automatic reaction

hypotheses.text: Sam is scared of the ball.
hypotheses.flaw: Fear would make her flinch away or freeze, and it would not explain why practice makes her faster or why tiredness makes her slower.

hypotheses.text: Signals travel along nerves from her eyes to her brain and spinal cord and out to her muscles; some pathways are short and automatic (reflexes), others go through decision-making and are slower but can be trained.
Sam's eyes are faster than other people's.
hypotheses.flaw: Eyes see at the same speed for everyone; what changes is how long the signal takes to turn into a movement — and eyes can't be made faster by drills.

hypotheses.text: She just guesses where the ball will go.
hypotheses.flaw: A guess is a decision, and decisions take time — the blink and the hands came before any guess was possible.

prediction.prompt: A shot is taken from close range, then from further and further away at the same speed. How does the time Sam has to react change as the shot gets closer?

second.question: Does practice make the blink reflex itself faster?

concepts.label: nerves carry signals
concepts.hint: What carries information from her eyes to her hands?

concepts.label: reflex: fast and automatic
concepts.hint: What do we call a reaction that skips the decision?

transfer.context: Dev touches a hot pan and his hand jerks away before he feels any pain.
options: His hand is used to heat.
A reflex pathway through his spinal cord moved his hand before the pain signal reached the part of his brain that notices it.
The pan was not really hot.
transfer.retryHint: The hand moved before he felt anything — which of Sam's clues was exactly like that?
transfer.explanation: The signal from Dev's hand reached his spinal cord, which sent a 'pull away' command straight back — the fast lane. The slower route to the thinking part of his brain, where pain is noticed, finished a moment later. That is why he moved before it hurt.

takeaway: Your nervous system has a fast lane and a thinking lane. Reflexes protect you before you can decide; decisions are slower but get faster with practice.
